name: Chest of drawers for DUX
description: A chest of drawers produced by DUX during the 1960s, constructed from bamboo and woven rattan. The front is arranged with two smaller drawers above two wider drawers, framed by rounded bamboo elements and wrapped corner details. The chest belongs to the broader tradition of colonial-style furniture, where bamboo, rattan and cane were used to create practical domestic pieces with an informal, warm expression. During the twentieth century, these materials became increasingly popular in European interiors, valued for their natural texture and association with lighter, more relaxed living environments. DUX was originally established as a specialist manufacturer of beds before broadening its production to include a wider range of domestic furniture. Over time, the company became closely associated with Swedish modernism, notably through its collaborations with designers such as Bruno Mathsson.

name: Chest of drawers 'Model RY 250' designed by Hans J. Wegner for Ry Møbler
description: The 'Model RY 250' chest of drawers designed by Hans J. Wegner and produced by Ry Møbler in Denmark in 1965 is veneered in rosewood, with four drawers, integrated metal handles and round legs in dark-stained solid oak. The model reflects Wegner’s precise understanding of proportion, craftsmanship and functional detail. Its surface is left visually uninterrupted, allowing the tone and grain of the rosewood to form the principal decoration. The drawer pulls are recessed into the front as circular cut-outs, each intersected by a flat horizontal metal bar. Rather than appearing as applied hardware, the handles are incorporated into the structure of the cabinet, turning a practical element into one of the design’s most distinctive visual features. Hans J. Wegner (1914–2007) was a Danish architect and furniture designer, widely regarded as one of the central figures of post-war Danish modernism. Trained as a cabinetmaker before studying architecture, he developed a practice rooted in construction, material knowledge and clarity of form. Stamped

name: Hall table
Sideboard 'Model FA 66' designed by Ib Kofod-Larsen
description: The clean lines of Ib Kofod-Larsen’s Model FA 66 in rosewood make it a notable Scandinavian mid-century collectable. Remarkably, it appears as if the elegant body balances on a separate cradle, but the base is in fact attached. Combining functionality with sophistication, the piece has four drawers and doors, each with concealed handles. Behind the first door are five beautifully made sliding drawers with visible mortise and tenon joints. The Danish designer Ib Kofod-Larsen frequently worked with high-quality woods such as rosewood, emphasising material and surface. He was one of the most influential furniture designers of his time; his designs, most famously the “Elizabeth” chair, are regarded as 20th-century design classics.

name: Bar cabinet
Sideboard 'Model B 598' designed by Josef Frank for Svenskt Tenn
description: This 'Model B 598' sideboard was designed by Josef Frank for Svenskt Tenn in Sweden during the 1950s. Executed in mahogany with a fine boxwood border, it combines generous storage with the lightness that characterises much of Frank’s furniture. The cabinet is raised on long, slender legs, allowing the rectangular drawer section to appear visually lighter despite its practical scale. Five drawers are fitted with brass handles, introducing a restrained decorative detail against the warm mahogany surface. The boxwood edging frames the piece with a subtle contrast, emphasising Frank’s interest in proportion, material warmth and domestic ease. Josef Frank developed an approach to interiors that stood apart from the stricter functionalism of the period. Frank favoured rooms and furniture that felt layered, comfortable and adaptable. After moving from Vienna to Sweden, Frank began working with Svenskt Tenn in 1934, where his furniture and textile designs became central to the company’s identity for several decades.

name: Bar cabinet designed by Kurt Østervig for KP Møbler
description: This rare Danish bar cabinet by Kurt Østervig for KP Møbler is a refined example of Scandinavian mid-century case furniture, combining disciplined proportions with thoughtful interior function. The exterior is finished in richly figured rosewood, where dramatic grain patterns bring movement and warmth to the façade. Shelving and drawers are arranged with precision, offering dedicated storage for bottles, glassware and accessories. Three drawers sit below the shelves, with the central drawer containing a recessed removable tray designed as a chessboard, executed in contrasting woods. Kurt Østervig (1912–1986) was one of the notable figures of Danish modern design. Originally trained as a shipbuilder, he brought a strong understanding of structure and proportion to his furniture. His work was exhibited internationally, including at the Milan Triennale during the 1950s, and examples of his designs are represented in the collection of the Museum of Modern Art in New York.

name: Sideboard designed by Erik Wørts for Kjellerup Møbelfabrik
description: This Danish sideboard by Erik Wørts for Kjellerup Møbelfabrik is a refined example of mid-century Scandinavian furniture, where practical storage is combined with disciplined proportions and carefully considered material contrast. The cabinet body is crafted in oak and the base and tapered legs are executed in wenge, introducing a darker visual anchor that emphasises the lightness of the upper form. The façade features a sliding door that conceals additional storage and reveals a more playful interior language through a set of drawers finished in contrasting lacquered colours, black and coral red. Erik Wørts (1916–1997) was an important contributor to the Danish modern movement, known for combining function with visual clarity. In the late 1950s he became one of the earliest professional designers engaged by Ingvar Kamprad, helping shape the formative identity of IKEA through practical, accessible furniture. Alongside this wider industrial work, he also produced more limited and finely executed designs for respected makers such as Kjellerup Møbelfabrik. This sideboard reflects that more specialised side of his practice, where craftsmanship and thoughtful detailing take centre stage.

name: Wall mounted cocktail cabinet designed by Svend Langkilde for Langkilde Møbler
description: This wall-mounted cocktail cabinet was designed by Svend Langkilde and produced by Langkilde Møbler in Denmark during the 1950s. Constructed in rosewood, the cabinet is defined by the expressive grain of the veneer, arranged across the doors to create a balanced and visually rich surface. Brass hinges, fittings and key details introduce a subtle contrast to the darker wood, emphasising the careful material pairing typical of Danish cabinetmaking from the period. The front opens through two doors with recessed handles, revealing a thoughtfully organised interior. Inside are shelves for storage, a small drawer for bar tools and accessories and a pull-out serving surface that extends the cabinet’s functionality when preparing drinks. Svend Langkilde (1911–1996) was a Danish cabinetmaker and designer associated with the international success of Danish Modern furniture in the mid-20th century. His work is characterised by refined craftsmanship and careful attention to materials and proportion. Langkilde received several distinctions during his career, including a Gold Medal at the Milan Triennale in 1957 and the Danish Industrial Design Award in 1962 and his work is represented in the collection of the Museum of Modern Art in New York.

name: Rosewood dresser designed by Henning Korch for CFC Silkeborg
description: This dresser was designed by Henning Korch for the cabinetmaker C.F. Christensen in Silkeborg. It is constructed in rosewood with expressive palisander veneer creating a continuous surface so the natural grain becomes a defining element of the piece. The façade is organised with a series of drawers, each fitted with small brass handles that offer a contrast to the depth and tone of the rosewood. Furniture produced in collaboration with the master cabinetmaker C.F. Christensen is particularly well regarded, combining precise craftsmanship with a refined understanding of wood. This dresser is a representative example of that partnership, where expressive rosewood veneer and discreet brass fittings are brought together in a functional piece firmly rooted in Danish mid century design.

name: Bar cabinet designed by Sture Lindholm for Per Jönssons Verkstäder
description: The cabinet is made of teak with darker-stained tapered legs. The front features two hinged doors with a central lock. Each door is decorated with an inlaid tin motif depicting a stylised profile head, one male and one female. The design reflects Swedish decorative arts of the early 1930s, combining elements associated with Swedish Grace, such as classical motifs and controlled ornamentation, with more simplified forms pointing toward early Scandinavian modernism. Sture Lindholm was a Swedish designer active primarily during the early 1930s. His work is known for combining restrained modern forms with decorative elements derived from classical and Art Deco sources. Lindholm’s furniture designs were produced in limited numbers, often as unique or near-unique pieces, and are today primarily known through surviving examples and later documentation. Per Jönssons Verkstäder was a Stockholm workshop known for high-quality craftsmanship and for executing small-scale productions for independent designers.

name: Shelf 'Book crib' model T-709 designed by Bruno Mathsson for Firma Karl Mathsson
description: Bruno Mathsson’s “Book crib” model T-709 is a refined example of Scandinavian vintage design where function and sculpture are perfectly aligned. Originally conceived in 1941, this piece was produced by Firma Karl Mathsson in 1964 and reflects the designer’s lifelong interest in reading, comfort and order. Crafted in solid birch with bent birch legs, the book crib has three angled compartments that cradle books, magazines or LPs while keeping the spines clearly visible and easy to reach. The splayed, tapering legs lift the form lightly from the floor, giving the piece an almost floating character. Bruno Mathsson (1907–1988) was a pioneering figure in Swedish modernism, celebrated for his mastery in combining functional design with a profound understanding of wood. His work seamlessly integrates craftsmanship and innovative thinking, as demonstrated in this shelving system, which perfectly captures the mid-century Scandinavian ideals of practicality, refinement, and flexibility.

name: Chest of drawers from the 'Triva' series designed for Nordiska Kompaniet
description: 'Trivia' series chest of drawers designed for Nordiska Kompaniet and produced in the company’s own workshop in Nyköping, Sweden. Executed in teak veneer with contrasting black lacquered metal frame and legs, it features three drawers fitted with distinctive circular brass pulls, with the original key retained. Introduced in 1945, the Triva series was conceived as a radical rethinking of furniture production and distribution. Developed from ideas by Elias Svedberg, whose flat-pack chair design won a competition in 1943, 'Triva' furniture was sold disassembled, pre-dating later flat-pack systems such as IKEA by nearly a decade. The series achieved immediate international success, widely distributed across Sweden and exhibited abroad in Paris, England and the United States, marking an important moment in the modernisation of Scandinavian furniture culture.

name: Storage box/container on wheels
description: Small rollable teak box Cubic shape with mitered edges and distinctive prong connections.

name: Pair of wall shelves
description: This pair of wall-mounted shelves was produced in Sweden during the 1950s. Each unit features a rectilinear open cube flanked by a horizontal shelf, creating a composition that is both geometric and functional. The back panels are finished in a dark contrasting tone, enhancing depth and subtly framing displayed objects. Surface wear is minimal and consistent with age, with the wood retaining a warm, even tone. The construction remains stable, though checking or reinforcing the mounting points is recommended prior to installation, particularly when intended for use with heavier objects. The design reflects the postwar Scandinavian approach to compact, functional domestic furniture, combining simplicity of form with thoughtful detailing.

name: Cabinet designed by Ole Wanscher for Illums Bolighus
description: This beautiful rosewood cabinet by Ole Wanscher was retailed through the established interior firm Illums Bolighus set in Copenhagen during the mid-20th century. The cabinet has vertically ribbed tambour doors that slide to either side, concealing the storage compartment behind. Below the doors is a row of drawers fitted with small brass pulls. The surfaces are flat and unadorned, with the emphasis placed on the precise joinery and wood grain. Ole Wanscher worked from the premise that furniture should be considered as part of a broader architectural interior rather than as isolated objects. Alongside his practice, he served as professor and later head of the furniture department at the Royal Academy of Fine Arts in Copenhagen, where he taught a generation of Danish designers. His work was informed by close study of historical furniture, including British and continental European models, as well as ancient sources, which he adapted to modern production.

name: Room divider
description: Originally a fixture in Magasin du Nord in Aarhus, Denmark. Magasin du Nord in Aarhus is a department store located in the heart of the city, offering a curated selection of fashion, beauty, homeware, and lifestyle products. It's part of the historic Danish Magasin du Nord chain, which dates back to the 19th century and is known for its elegant stores and quality-focused retail experience.

name: Cabinet model 2135 designed by Josef Frank for Svenskt Tenn
description: The cabinet stands on slender legs, maintaining an airy, lightweight appearance that aligns with Frank’s preference for furniture that feels open rather than heavy or imposing. Josef Frank’s design philosophy, which emphasised both practicality and visual harmony, is evident in the cabinet’s thoughtful proportions and refined material choices. The combination of cherry wood and root veneer aligns with his preference for natural materials, celebrating their beauty while ensuring a timeless piece. Model 2135 was made in two versions—one with this striking root veneer and the other with simple mahogany doors. Simplicity and exceptional quality make this piece a timeless Svenskt Tenn collectible. Josef Frank was an Austrian-Swedish architect and designer known for his vibrant, functional, and timeless furniture and textiles. Rejecting strict modernism, he embraced colour, pattern, and organic forms, creating designs that felt warm and inviting. His work with Svenskt Tenn shaped Scandinavian design, blending craftsmanship with a playful, effortless elegance.

name: Bedside table model 914 designed by Josef Frank for Svenskt Tenn,
description: Josef Frank’s Model 914 bedside table, designed in the 1950s for Svenskt Tenn, reflects his thoughtful approach to practical and well-balanced design. Made from mahogany, it has a rectangular top, a single drawer with a brass handle, and a lower open shelf. Its versatile form allows it to complement a variety of interiors. Frank designed around 2,000 pieces of furniture for Svenskt Tenn, and this bedside table is part of that legacy.

name: Sideboard designed by Josef Frank for Svenskt Tenn
description: This stunning sideboard, designed by Josef Frank for Svenskt Tenn in the 1950s, reflects the designer's innovative approach to modernism, where comfort and artistry take precedence over strict minimalism. Frank’s designs are celebrated for their timeless appeal and human-centered aesthetic. Crafted from luxurious pyramid mahogany with boxwood inlays, the sideboard is accented with brass details, creating a harmonious balance of materials. The rich textures and warm tones of the pyramid mahogany add depth and character, making this piece a striking focal point in any room. Modernity can provide a shipping quote upon request—just let us know the destination. We’re also happy to share additional photos, videos, or details as needed.

name: Serving trolley model 889 designed by Josef Frank for Svenskt Tenn, Sweden
description: The trolley, model 889, by Josef Frank is a prime example of design from the Swedish Grace movement. The design of the trolley references neoclassicism, drawing inspiration from objects found in Ancient Greece and Rome. The brass edge on this piece, featuring perforated decorative holes and scalloped detailing, would likely be made using a combination of stamping, perforating, and forming techniques. Josef Frank's works are held in several prestigious museum collections, including that of the Nationalmuseum, Stockholm, the Wien Museum, the MOMA and Cooper Hewitt in New York, and the V&A in London. The piece was made and sold by Svenskt Tenn, an iconic Swedish design company, founded in 1924 by Estrid Ericson. In 1934, Ericson partnered with Josef Frank, an Austrian-born architect and designer who had fled rising political tensions in Europe. Their partnership lasted 33 years.

name: Shelf  'Book crib' model T-709 designed by Bruno Mathsson for Firma Karl Mathsson, Sweden
description: Bruno Mathsson’s "Book Crib" model T-709 exemplifies the seamless blend of functionality and artistic form that defines Scandinavian design. First conceived in 1941 and produced by Firma Karl Mathsson in 1964, this piece highlights Mathsson’s passion for creating practical, well-organized spaces for reading and relaxation. Made from solid birch with gracefully bent birch legs, the book crib features three angled compartments designed to neatly hold books, magazines, or LPs, keeping the spines visible and easily accessible. The gently splayed legs give the piece an airy, almost suspended quality, a hallmark of Swedish modernism during this era. Bruno Mathsson (1907–1988) was a pioneering figure in Swedish modernism, celebrated for his mastery in combining functional design with a profound understanding of wood. His work seamlessly integrates craftsmanship and innovative thinking, as demonstrated in this shelving system, which perfectly captures the mid-century Scandinavian ideals of practicality, refinement, and flexibility. Stamped.

name: Serving trolley model 2777 designed by Josef Frank for Svenskt Tenn
description: Josef Frank’s model 2777 serving trolley, designed in the 1950s, was crafted from mahogany and features a sleek black Arborite top with the same material used on both shelves below the surface. It has brass handles that add an elegant contrast and enhance its sophistication. The trolley's design reflects Frank's modernist aesthetic, balancing function and style.

name: Rosewood bar table by Leif Alring
Chest of drawers attributed to Ib Kofod-Larsen for Illums Bolighus
description: This chest of drawers, attributed to Ib Kofod-Larsen and produced for Illums Bolighus in the 1960s, reflects the refined restraint of Danish modern furniture. Executed in richly grained rosewood, the cabinet is defined by its clear geometry and balanced proportions. Five drawers are arranged within a compact rectangular body, their fronts emphasising the expressive natural pattern of the wood. The chest stands on slender, tapered legs that lift the cabinet lightly from the floor, a characteristic feature of Scandinavian design from this period. The recessed drawer fronts contribute to the clean, uninterrupted surface of the façade, allowing the material itself to become the primary visual element. The result is a piece that combines practical storage with the quiet elegance associated with Danish cabinetmaking of the mid-twentieth century. Ib Kofod-Larsen (1921–2003) was one of the central figures of Danish modernism. His furniture is recognised for its sculptural clarity, careful proportions, and refined craftsmanship, often highlighting the natural beauty of woods such as teak and rosewood. Produced by several leading Scandinavian manufacturers, his designs remain admired for their enduring simplicity and material sensitivity. Metal 'Illums Bolighus' retailer tag attached.

name: Chest of drawers model 146 designed by Carl-Axel Acking for Svenska Möbelfabriken
description: This chest of drawers, model 146, was designed by Carl Axel Acking in the 1940s and produced by Svenska Möbelfabriken in Bodafors. Executed in elm with richly patterned root veneer across the drawer fronts, the piece is distinguished by the expressive, marbled character of the wood. The root veneer creates a lively surface that contrasts subtly with the calmer grain of the surrounding frame, highlighting the cabinet’s careful material composition. During the 1940s, Svenska Möbelfabriken in Bodafors was among Sweden’s most progressive furniture manufacturers, collaborating with several of the country’s leading designers. Through partnerships with figures such as Carl Axel Acking, Bruno Mathsson and Carl Malmsten, the company produced furniture that helped shape the development of Swedish modern design. Carl Axel Acking (1910–2001) was a prominent Swedish architect and designer whose work contributed significantly to the development of Scandinavian modernism. Trained in both architecture and applied arts, he worked across furniture, textiles, interiors and architecture, consistently emphasising clarity of form and sensitivity to materials. His designs combine functional purpose with a restrained elegance that continues to define the legacy of Swedish mid-century design.

name: Dresser and Mirror set designed by Aksel Kjersgaard, Denmark
Sideboard for Lysberg, Hansen & Therp
Cabinet
Shelf designed by Alvar Andersson for Hyresgästernas Möbelaffär
Cabinet designed by Ib Kofod-Larsen
description: This cabinet by Ib Kofod-Larsen is a refined example of Danish modern furniture from the 1960s. Executed in teak, the design highlights the wood’s warm tone and expressive grain. The piece features four drawers arranged within a clean, rectangular cabinet body, each fitted with a round wooden knob. The elevated base is typical of mid-century Scandinavian furniture, where visual balance and practical proportions were central considerations. Ib Kofod-Larsen (1921–2003) was one of the key designers associated with Danish modernism. Known for his elegant furniture forms, he worked extensively with teak and rosewood, creating pieces that balanced sculptural clarity with a strong emphasis on craftsmanship. His designs were produced by several respected Danish manufacturers and remain widely recognised for their enduring simplicity and quality. Marked.

name: Sideboard model 1148 designed by Josef Frank for Svenskt Tenn
description: This sideboard, model 1148, was designed by Josef Frank in the 1950s for Svenskt Tenn and reflects the designer’s characteristic balance between elegance and practicality. Executed in walnut with surfaces in richly patterned alder root veneer, the piece combines restrained structural lines with gently curved details. The sides are fitted with drop-leaf flaps, allowing the surface to be extended when needed. The front is arranged with six drawers: a wide upper drawer followed by two medium-sized drawers and three smaller drawers below. Brass drop handles provide a refined decorative accent, while a discreet central lock secures the drawers. Frank often combined luxurious veneers with more understated structural woods, creating a subtle contrast that emphasises both craftsmanship and material quality. Josef Frank (1885–1967) was an Austrian-born architect, designer, and artist who later became a Swedish citizen. After moving to Sweden in the 1930s, he began a long collaboration with Estrid Ericson and her company Svenskt Tenn, where he developed a distinctive design language that merged Viennese elegance with the functional ideals of Scandinavian modernism. His furniture, textiles and interiors remain among the most celebrated expressions of twentieth-century Swedish design.

name: Shelving system designed by Bruno Mathsson for Mathsson International
description: This wall-mounted shelving system, designed by Bruno Mathsson and produced by Mathsson International in the 1960s, embodies the principles of Scandinavian design with its elegant simplicity and functional versatility. Crafted from beech, the design features slender shelves that rest on gently curved wooden brackets, which extend from vertical wall-mounted rails. Mathsson’s modular shelving system was created with adaptability in mind. It offers the flexibility to combine shelves of different depths and spacing to suit various needs, with the deeper angled lower shelf specifically designed to showcase magazines or books in a face-out position. Additionally, white lacquered steel bars are included for easy direct wall mounting. Bruno Mathsson (1907–1988) was a pioneering figure in Swedish modernism, celebrated for his mastery in combining functional design with a profound understanding of wood. His work seamlessly integrates craftsmanship and innovative thinking, as demonstrated in this shelving system, which perfectly captures the mid-century Scandinavian ideals of practicality, refinement and flexibility.

name: Wall cabinet
Set of eight shelves
description: Stackable.

name: Shelving unit 'K5 wall shelf Type 1' designed by Claesson Koivisto Rune for ADX
Shelving unit 'K5 wall shelf Type 2' designed by Claesson Koivisto Rune for ADX
Shelving unit 'K5 wall shelf Type 3' designed by Claesson Koivisto Rune for ADX
Sewing box designed by Magnus L. Stephensen for Axel Søllner
description: Magnus Læssøe Stephensen was a renowned mid-century Danish architect whose revolutionary approach to design did away with the extravagant flourishes of the time. Inspired by the simplicity of Bauhaus and Japanese arts and crafts, Stephensen's designs focused on clean lines and practicality. His furniture designs were highly functional with a strong respect for craftsmanship - an aesthetic that has since become synonymous with Scandinavian design. Stamped.

name: Cabinet ‘Hug’ designed by Rasmus Appel
Wall hung cabinet for A. Lagerberg
description: An expressive allmoge inspired cabinet that reflects the late 19th century Swedish interest in vernacular craft, a direction championed by designers and workshops such as A. Lagerberg. The piece belongs to the same cultural moment in which Stockholm’s exhibitions of the 1890s highlighted a growing curiosity for new European ideas, alongside a reassessment of national traditions. Constructed in warm stained wood, the cabinet features open shelving above a lower storage section with paneled doors. Carved foliate ornaments and painted details in green and red contribute to its strong visual identity, closely related to the Scandinavian interpretation of early l’art nouveau. Turned supports, arched cutouts, and delicate sculptural accents show the influence of artisans who were moving beyond strict neo Renaissance and neo Rococo models that had dominated Swedish furniture production in the preceding decades. The workshop of A. Lagerberg, later known for assisting Ellen Key with her program exhibitions at the Stockholm Workers’ Institute, stood at the forefront of this shift toward a more expressive and modern sensibility. This cabinet illustrates that transition. It draws on rustic allmoge motifs while engaging with the new decorative languages emerging across Europe at the time. Overall, the piece stands as a distinctive example of Swedish craft at the turn of the century, rooted in tradition yet shaped by a progressive artistic vision. Presented at the Stockholm Exhibition of 1897.

name: Wall cupboard designed by Lars Larsson and Stig Lönngren for HI-Gruppen
description: Wall cupboard in lacquered birch plywood. Closed, the piece presents as a compact, pared-back volume. Once opened, it reveals a series of trays allowing for efficient storage and easy access within a limited space. A vertical metal rod contributes to the structure and organisation of the interior, with a mirror integrated into the upper section. The design emphasises functionality and economy of means, in line with Swedish design approaches of the 1960s. HI-Gruppen was founded in Stockholm in 1957 by interior architect Stig Lönngren. It brought together interior architects, furniture designers and craftsmen with the aim of reasserting the role of craft within the design process, while allowing for experimentation outside the constraints of industrial production. The group produced high-quality furniture, often conceived with potential industrial production in mind. Their first exhibition took place in 1960, and pieces were numbered sequentially. HI-Gruppen remained active until 1972. Possibly unique.
